text: Course 5 introduced gs.info, gs.warn, and gs.error as the real server-side logging APIs. For an integration script, where and what you log with them matters enormously, because an integration fails at 3 a.m., unattended, and the only record of what happened is whatever got written to the log at the time. A vague message tells the person troubleshooting it at 9 a.m. almost nothing — which integration, which record, which call, what status code, what was different about this run versus the thousand that worked fine. None of that is captured, so the first hour of any investigation becomes reconstructing context logging could have recorded for free.

Here's the anti-pattern in code: a try block calls execute, and the catch block logs the single string 'Error occurred.' Technically that is a log entry. Practically, it answers none of the questions a real investigation needs — not which city, not which status code, not whether this has happened before.

A well-instrumented script logs at three specific moments. Before sending the request, so a stuck or slow run is visible while it's still in progress. After receiving the response, logging at least the HTTP status code, so a successful run leaves a trail too. And when an error occurs, logging the specific status code, the specific record or parameter involved, and enough context to reconstruct what was different about this one failure.

This version logs before the call with the city, logs again after the call with the status code, and on failure calls gs.error with a template string using curly-brace placeholders — zero, one, two — filled in order by city, status code, and the response body. That's real, supported syntax on gs.info, gs.warn, and gs.error, and it is the entire difference between a five-minute log review later and an hour of guesswork, because every value a future investigation needs is already sitting in the log line itself.

Beyond your own gs.* calls, IntegrationHub keeps its own execution log for spoke actions and custom actions — the same idea as Course 4's Flow execution log: a record of each run's inputs, which step it reached, and what the output or error was at each step. When a custom spoke action fails, check that execution log first — it narrows down exactly where in your script to look next. Next lesson puts backoff, idempotency, and structured logging together in one real, worked error-handling lab.
